topic: 1667: A Terminal UI for Writing Fiction with Language Models

key_points: The subject itself: a full-screen keyboard-driven TUI ('1667 writing environment, terminal') that asks a model for the next paragraph and keeps every take; tagline 'write your novel in the terminal'.

Install: `curl -fsSL https://1667.ai/install.sh | sh` installs 0.10.9 (macOS arm64/x64, glibc 2.17+ Linux arm64/x64); PowerShell installer for Windows x64; `npm install --global @1667-ai/cli@latest` (Node 22); source build needs Bun 1.3.14+ and Node 22. Optional GitHub-attestation verification path for the installer.

Core model: a story is made of parts; each part can hold several takes; the selected take at each point forms the story line; the map has three views — path (selected line), tree (where the story branches), mass (all takes sorted by size/date/depth/name).
Story-line tags: Canon, Alt, Draft, Discarded, Summary; only one Canon line per story (setting a new Canon demotes the earlier one to Alt).

Facts: notes (characters, places, items, rules) that enter requests — 'always' Facts enter every continuation, 'keyed' Facts enter when a key matches recent story text or the instruction; Facts can have per-story-part states and can be lensed in the tree view.

Context control: a context meter showing exact (8.1k), near-exact (≈8.1k) or estimated (~8.1k) token counts, plus `Ctrl+R` request viewer that shows the model, messages, Facts, token counts and context window (never credentials).

Privacy claims: 'analytics not collected, telemetry not collected, crash reporter errors stay in a local log, install ID none, account not required'; the only network side-effect admitted is a background npm update check that can be turned off.
40 keyboard commands; the site highlights 8 for a full session: space (continue), Enter (direct), ←/→ (flip takes), ↑/↓ (move parts), r (retake), w (write a take yourself), e (edit), m (map).

Model support: OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, KoboldCpp, plus a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint; starting generation defaults temperature 0.8, max output tokens 2,048, context window 32,768 (configurable 1–1,000k).

Provider secrets are saved on-device ('never stored on our servers' per the settings screen); projects live in a folder you choose and export writes the selected story line to Markdown in the same folder; a Vault Password can seal project files at rest.

Open source under Apache-2.0 — the decisive structural difference from every commercial tool in this comparison; repo description: 'A full-screen terminal environment for writing fiction with language models.'
GitHub API (fetched this run): 26 stars, 0 forks, 7 open issues, language TypeScript, created 2026-08-04, last pushed 2026-09-29, not archived, 0 watchers/subscribers.

Topics are a compact statement of intent: ai-writing, bun, creative-writing, fiction-writing, generative-ai, large-language-models, llm-harness, local-llm, loom, novel, sillytavern, story-tree, terminal, terminal-ui, tui, typescript, writing-tool.
README positioning: 'Write story parts, keep alternative takes, and select the story line that you want to read. Connect a model when you want generated prose, or write every take yourself.'

Docs set beyond the website: story-storage, model-providers, generation-boundaries, summary-branches, story-line-copy-paste, autoname, platforms and standalone builds, technical terms, SillyTavern import, character-card import, Generation Profile transfer.

CHANGELOG 'Unreleased' shows scope expanding past the terminal: a new experimental `1667 web` command that serves a local Library/manuscript page (with 1667's own story-part and take navigation) and a **desktop app** shipping its own fonts and app icon in 0.11.0-beta.5.

CHANGELOG provider notes are a useful tell about maintenance velocity: it tracks new model names (e.g. Claude Opus/Fable/Mythos entries, ChatGPT-plan model lists) and drops models that no longer work.

Closest philosophical rival for serious novelists: closed-source SaaS built around a Codex (living story bible for characters, locations, lore, timelines), planning modes for outlining, and bring-your-own-key AI integration.
Pricing (2026, secondary sources): $4/mo Scribe, $8/mo Hobbyist, $14/mo Artisan, $20/mo Specialist, with BYOK meaning the real bill = subscription + your own API usage (two vendors, one workflow).
21-day free trial, no permanently free tier.
Where it beats 1667: browser/desktop UI, story bible tooling, planning workflows. Where 1667 answers it: no subscription at all, Apache-2.0 source, local files, no account.

Relevant to the 'branching takes' claim: NovelCrafter's story bible is a per-scene context mechanism, not a take-comparison tree — the HN thread's 'track changes in a git-like narrative tree' request is exactly the gap 1667 targets.
The market's best-known fiction-specific platform; its own 2026 posts position a proprietary fiction-trained model (Muse) plus integrations as the differentiator from generic chat models.

Pricing (secondary sources, 2026): roughly $10–$44/mo with generation on paid tiers described as credit-based in some comparisons; closed source; Story Bible notes are manual rather than AI-extracted per one comparison table.

Marketing line that 1667 implicitly contests: 'purpose-built for novelists with specialized tools that understand story structure, character voice, and narrative pacing — something general-purpose AI can't match.' 1667's counter is model-agnosticism (any OpenAI-compatible/Anthropic/local endpoint) plus visible prompts.
Cited as the standard recommendation in 2026 roundups (Joanna Penn/Brandon Sanderson mentions appear in comparison posts) — useful as the 'what most writers will compare 1667 against' baseline.
Closed source and cloud-hosted: no source audit, no local-only mode, and story text necessarily leaves the machine.
Long-running subscription service known for its own fine-tuned story models and Lorebook context system; $10/mo entry tier per 2026 comparisons, closed source, trial-only rather than free.
Strong in interactive fiction and world-building; one 2026 comparison scores it as the best pick for interactive fiction, another emphasises its retry history and lore/context tooling.
Direct migration target for 1667 — the docs include a 'Move from NovelAI' page and the app imports NovelAI archives (stories, scenarios, Lorebooks, presets, retry history).
Contrast to draw: NovelAI sells a model + hosted runtime; 1667 sells no model and runs no server, so cost is $0 plus whatever provider (or local GPU) you already have.

The open-source neighbour in the local-model writing space: 'LLM Frontend for Power Users', AGPL-3.0, JavaScript, created 2023-02-09, last pushed 2026-09-23, and by far the biggest community in this set — 33,976 stars (GitHub API, fetched this run).
Different product shape: a chat/roleplay frontend (character cards, group chats, Character Books, World Info, presets) — generative conversation, not a manuscript with parts and takes.

Backend overlap is nearly total: both target Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, KoboldCpp and OpenAI-compatible endpoints, which makes 1667's SillyTavern import (chats, cards, Character Books, World Info) the practical on-ramp for that crowd.
Useful anchor claim for the review: the local-model fiction audience is large (33,976 stars) while 1667's repo is at 26 stars and 0 forks — early-project context that keeps the comparison honest.
2026 guide content around SillyTavern is dominated by local setup guides (KoboldCpp, Ollama, LM Studio) and privacy framing ('no cloud, no logging'), which is the same buyer 1667 is pitching.

angles: The thread is the story: 1667's Show HN turned into a referendum on AI in creative writing rather than a tool review. The builder reported 'a lot of hate mail' and anxiety over the reception, then reframed the app as 'a form of low tech holodeck' for writing the pulp fiction 'no one writes anymore.' A review that reports that split honestly — craft-defence vs tool-defence — is the differentiated angle, because every competing 2026 roundup is a feature table with affiliate links.

The strongest critique in the thread is not moral but mechanical: if you choose what happens next before the model writes it, what are you actually getting? The reply that survives it is the tree/branch model — many takes, keep the one that works — so evaluate 1667 on whether take-comparison (←/→ between siblings, word-count mass view) genuinely serves that, or just moves the same decision one step later.

Terminal-first and offline-first as an identity, not a gimmick: no account, no telemetry, no install ID, Apache-2.0, project files in a folder you own, vault-password sealing, OS-level single-writer lock. Contrast with every hosted rival where story text must leave the machine.

Context control is the real craft feature: Facts (always vs keyed), per-story-part Fact states, a context meter that distinguishes exact/near-exact/estimated token counts, and a request viewer (Ctrl+R) that shows exactly what is sent. The thesis is 'no invisible prompt' — testable, and a clean counterpoint to closed tools that silently summarise or auto-drop context.

The feature HN writers actually asked for: one commenter wanted 'track changes in a git-like, narrative-tree way' and said if somebody improved on track changes that way it would be genuinely useful for working writers. 1667 is the closest thing shipped to that request — worth stating as the article's central verdict rather than a spec dump.

Migration as an on-ramp: the app imports SillyTavern chats, character cards, Character Books and World Info, and NovelAI archives (stories, scenarios, Lorebooks, presets, retry history). For the 33,976-star local-model crowd this is the practical 'how do I try it without losing my lore' answer.

Honest pre-1.0 caveats that most roundups hide: 26 stars, 0 forks, 7 open issues, stable 0.10.9 while 0.11.0-beta.5 is in flight, terminal-only learning curve (40 commands), and a CHANGELOG showing the terminal-only promise already bending toward an experimental `1667 web` page and a desktop app.

Who it is not for: writers who want an editor, planner, agentic multi-scene drafting, publishing pipelines or cloud sync. 1667 generates one paragraph when asked and then waits — that is the design, not a missing feature, and saying so plainly is more useful than a feature-count comparison.

The publishing-ethics backdrop that any AI-fiction review now needs: KDP-era disclosure expectations, the 54%-experimented vs 11%-regular-use gap among professional authors, fiction authors being markedly warier than non-fiction writers, and the Authors Guild's consent/compensation line (90%). Frame 1667 as a personal-use tool inside that debate, not a slop-pipeline enabler — which is exactly how its author framed it.
